items.prompt: How does an octopus change the colour of its skin so quickly?

options.label: Tiny muscle-controlled sacs of pigment expand and contract
options.feedback: Called chromatophores, these sacs are stretched wide open or squeezed nearly shut by a ring of muscles, changing how much colour shows.

options.label: It secretes a coloured dye onto its skin
options.feedback: No dye is released onto the surface; the colour change happens inside the skin itself, not on top of it.

options.label: Its blood changes colour and shows through the skin
options.feedback: An octopus's blood does carry an unusual colour, but that has nothing to do with the rapid colour changes seen on its skin.

options.label: It slowly grows new, differently coloured skin
options.feedback: Growing new skin would take far too long; the change seen here happens almost instantly, not over days.

items.ok_line: Muscles stretching pigment sacs open and shut, faster than growth ever could.
items.ko_line: Think about what could make a colour appear or vanish in a fraction of a second.
items.exp_text: An octopus's skin is packed with tiny sacs called chromatophores, each one holding a dot of pigment and ringed by a set of muscles. When those muscles contract, they stretch the sac wide and spread the pigment into a broad patch of colour; when they relax, the sac shrinks back down and the colour nearly disappears. Because muscles react almost instantly, an octopus can shift its pattern across its whole body in a heartbeat.

items.prompt: How can an octopus squeeze its whole body through a gap barely wider than one of its eyes?

options.label: It has no rigid skeleton apart from its beak
options.feedback: With nothing hard inside it except the beak, its soft body can flow and reshape itself to fit almost any opening the beak can pass through.

options.label: It can temporarily dissolve part of its body
options.feedback: No part of the body is dissolved; the whole animal stays intact while its soft tissue simply reshapes itself.

options.label: It shrinks by pushing water out through its skin
options.feedback: Water is not stored inside the body in a way that could be pushed out through the skin to shrink it.

options.label: Its arms detach and reattach on the other side
options.feedback: The arms stay firmly attached the whole time; it is the body's soft shape, not detachment, that allows the squeeze.

items.ok_line: One hard beak, and a body that can flow around anything else.
items.ko_line: Think about what part of an octopus's body is actually hard.
items.exp_title: A body with only one hard part
items.exp_text: Nearly everything inside an octopus is soft, muscular tissue, with a single exception: its beak, the one part that cannot be squeezed any smaller. Since the beak sets the true limit on what the animal can pass through, an octopus tests a gap with its beak first, and if that fits, the rest of its soft, boneless body can be pulled and reshaped to follow. That is why an octopus can pour itself through an opening that looks impossibly small for its size.

items.prompt: How does a squid dart away suddenly from danger?

options.label: By forcing water out through a narrow siphon
options.feedback: Water drawn into the body is squeezed out fast through this narrow tube, thrusting the squid in the opposite direction.

options.label: By flapping its fins rapidly like a bird's wings
options.feedback: Its fins help with steady swimming and steering, but a sudden dart of speed comes from a different, more forceful method.

options.label: By inflating with air to shoot to the surface
options.feedback: A squid has no way to fill itself with air, and moving quickly away from danger does not mean rising toward the surface.

options.label: By releasing a burst of bubbles from its skin
options.feedback: No bubbles are released from the skin; the sudden burst of speed comes from forcing water, not air, out of the body.

items.ok_line: A forceful jet of water, pushing the squid the opposite way.
items.ko_line: Think about what a squid could forcefully push out of its body to shoot itself backward.
items.exp_title: Jetting away on a squeeze of water
items.exp_text: A squid draws water into a muscular cavity inside its body, then suddenly clamps that cavity shut, forcing the water out fast through a narrow, flexible tube called a siphon. Pushing water out one way thrusts the squid's body the opposite way, giving it a sudden burst of speed far quicker than paddling with fins could manage. By aiming the siphon in different directions, the squid can jet forward, backward, or off to the side as the moment demands.

items.prompt: How does a clam manage to clamp its shell shut so tightly that it is very hard to pry open?

options.label: A pair of strong muscles pull the two shell halves together
options.feedback: These muscles, anchored to each half of the shell, contract to hold the two sides pressed firmly shut.

options.label: A sticky glue seals the shell's edges
options.feedback: No glue is involved; the shell is held shut by muscular force, which is also why it can be reopened at will.

options.label: Water pressure outside pushes the shell closed
options.feedback: Outside water pressure acts equally on the whole shell and cannot by itself pull two hinged halves together.

options.label: The hinge itself locks rigidly in place
options.feedback: The hinge only allows the shell to pivot; it is the muscles pulling against it that actually hold the shell shut.

items.ok_line: Muscle, not glue or a rigid lock, is what does the clamping.
items.ko_line: Think about what could pull two hinged shell halves together and hold them there.
items.exp_title: Muscle strong enough to hold a hinge shut
items.exp_text: A clam's two shell halves are joined at a hinge, and one or two thick adductor muscles run across the inside, anchored to each half. When these muscles contract, they pull the two halves toward each other and hold them clamped shut for as long as the muscle keeps contracting. Because this grip depends on active muscle rather than a fixed lock, the shell can also be prised open once the muscle finally tires or is cut.

items.prompt: As a hermit crab's body grows too large for its borrowed shell, how does it get a new one?

options.label: It searches out and moves into a larger empty shell
options.feedback: Since it cannot grow its own shell, it must instead find one left behind by another snail and switch into it.

options.label: It grows its own new shell around the old one
options.feedback: A hermit crab makes no shell of its own at all; borrowing one already left behind by a snail is its only option.

options.label: It stretches its current shell wider using acid
options.feedback: The shell it lives in belonged to another animal and cannot be reshaped from the inside by any means.

options.label: It simply lives without a shell from then on
options.feedback: Going shell-less would leave its soft abdomen exposed to injury and predators, so the crab keeps searching for a fitting replacement instead.

items.ok_line: A new home found ready-made, since it cannot build one of its own.
items.ko_line: Remember that the shell was never the crab's own to begin with.
items.exp_title: Trading up to a borrowed home
items.exp_text: A hermit crab has a soft, curled abdomen and no shell of its own, so it lives inside the empty shell of a sea snail instead, carrying it everywhere for protection. As the crab grows, that shell no longer has room, and the crab must search out and try a larger empty shell before finally backing out of the old one and into the new. Because suitable empty shells are not always easy to come by, several crabs will sometimes line up by size and swap shells one after another in a single exchange.

items.prompt: How can a crab regrow a claw it has lost in a fight or to a predator?

options.label: A small new limb bud grows back and develops with each moult
options.feedback: A tiny bud forms at the wound and is carried, growing a little further, through each successive shedding of the shell.

options.label: It cannot regrow a lost claw at all
options.feedback: A crab can in fact regrow a lost claw, though the new one only reaches full size gradually, moult by moult.

options.label: It transplants tissue from its other claw
options.feedback: No tissue moves from one limb to another; the new claw grows entirely from a bud at the site of the loss.

options.label: A new claw appears fully grown the instant the old one is lost
options.feedback: The new claw starts out small and only reaches its full size gradually, through a series of moults rather than all at once.

items.ok_line: A little further with each shedding of the shell, until it matches the rest.
items.ko_line: Think about what has to happen to a crab's whole body for anything on it to grow larger.
items.exp_text: When a crab loses a claw, a small bud of new tissue begins forming at the wound almost right away, tucked beneath the shell that still covers the stump. Because a crab's hard shell does not stretch, this bud can only grow larger each time the crab moults and briefly has a soft, expandable covering, so the new claw is carried a little further along with every shed shell. Over several moults, the claw gradually reaches a size close to matching the one it replaced.

items.prompt: A lobster's shell cannot stretch. How does the lobster inside it manage to grow bigger over time?

options.label: It periodically sheds its old shell for a larger new one
options.feedback: Underneath, a soft new shell has already formed; once the old one splits away, the lobster swells before that new shell hardens.

options.label: The shell slowly stretches along with the lobster's body
options.feedback: A hardened shell cannot stretch at all; a lobster's growth is only possible because it periodically leaves that shell behind.

options.label: It grows only outward, folding extra body over the old shell
options.feedback: There is no folding of new growth over an old, unshed shell; growth instead happens only after the old shell is fully cast off.

options.label: New shell segments are added like rings on a tree
options.feedback: A lobster's shell is not built up in added rings; it is entirely replaced from time to time instead.

items.ok_line: Growth happens all at once, in the short window after the old shell splits away.
items.ko_line: Think about what has to happen to a rigid shell before the body inside it can get any bigger.
items.exp_title: Growing between one shell and the next
items.exp_text: A lobster's hard shell holds its exact shape and size and cannot expand along with the growing body inside it. Beneath that old shell, a soft, wrinkled new one gradually forms, and when the old shell finally splits open and is shed, the lobster rapidly draws in water to swell its body before the new shell has time to harden. Over the following days that new shell stiffens in place, locking in the lobster's larger size until the next time it moults.

items.prompt: What is a mollusc's radula used for?

options.label: Rasping and scraping food loose to be eaten
options.feedback: Lined with many tiny, tooth-like ridges, it works much like a file, dragged back and forth over food to tear off small pieces.

options.label: Filtering plankton out of passing water
options.feedback: Filtering water for plankton is handled by other structures, such as gills, in the molluscs that feed that way.

options.label: Sensing chemicals dissolved in the water
options.feedback: Sensing dissolved chemicals is a job for tentacles or other sensory organs, not for this ridged, food-scraping structure.

options.label: Pumping water in and out for movement
options.feedback: Moving by jetting water is managed elsewhere in the body; this structure plays no part in propulsion.

items.ok_line: A tongue-like file, dragged across food to tear it loose.
items.ko_line: Picture a small, ridged, tongue-like band dragged back and forth over a surface.
items.exp_title: A tongue lined with tiny teeth
items.exp_text: Many molluscs, including snails and slugs, carry a ribbon-like structure in the mouth called a radula, covered in rows of small, hard, tooth-like points. Muscles drag this ribbon back and forth over a leaf, algae, or other food, and the tiny points scrape and tear off small fragments with each pass, much like a file working across a rough surface. As the front rows of teeth wear down from use, they are steadily replaced by new rows growing in further back.

items.prompt: How does a scallop suddenly swim away from a threat, unlike most other bivalves that stay fixed in place?

options.label: It claps its two shells together, forcing out jets of water
options.feedback: Snapping the shells shut squeezes water out on either side of the hinge, thrusting the scallop through the water.

options.label: It grows temporary fins along the shell's edge
options.feedback: No fins grow on a scallop's shell; the sudden swimming comes entirely from the shells snapping together.

options.label: It releases a puff of gas to float away
options.feedback: No gas is released to carry a scallop off; its escape depends on forcefully clapping its shells, not on floating.

options.label: It crawls rapidly using a muscular foot
options.feedback: Many other bivalves do use a muscular foot to creep slowly along, but a scallop's sudden escape is a rapid swim, not a crawl.

items.ok_line: Each clap of the shell pushes out a jet strong enough to carry the scallop away.
items.ko_line: Think about what forceful, repeated movement of the two shells could push against the water.
items.exp_title: Swimming by clapping its own shell
items.exp_text: Unlike most bivalves, a scallop is not fixed to a rock or buried in sediment, and it can snap its two shell halves rapidly shut over and over. Each snap squeezes a jet of water out near the shell's hinge, and that forceful jet pushes the scallop's whole body through the water in the opposite direction. Repeating the clap again and again lets it flee in a rapid, jerky burst whenever a starfish or other slow predator draws near.

items.prompt: How does a barnacle feed while staying permanently fixed to a single spot on a rock?

options.label: It sweeps feathery, leg-like limbs through the water to catch food
options.feedback: These limbs, called cirri, comb repeatedly through the passing water, catching plankton and fine particles drifting by.

options.label: It slowly drags itself along the rock to find fresh food
options.feedback: An adult barnacle stays cemented in one place for life and cannot drag itself anywhere to search for food.

options.label: It absorbs dissolved nutrients directly through its shell
options.feedback: Its hard outer shell does not absorb nutrients; catching food instead relies on limbs reaching out from an opening at the top.

options.label: It waits for the tide to wash food directly into its mouth
options.feedback: Food is actively swept in by the barnacle's own limbs rather than simply arriving on its own with the tide.

items.ok_line: Feathery limbs doing the reaching, since the body itself cannot move at all.
items.ko_line: Think about what a fixed, cemented animal could still move, even if its whole body cannot travel anywhere.
items.exp_title: Legs that do the travelling the body cannot
items.exp_text: An adult barnacle cements itself to a rock or another hard surface and stays there permanently, unable to crawl off in search of food the way many other creatures can. From an opening at the top of its shell, it repeatedly extends a set of feathery, leg-like limbs called cirri, sweeping them through the surrounding water to snag drifting plankton and fine particles. Pulling the catch back inside with each sweep, the barnacle manages to feed steadily despite never leaving the single spot it is fixed to.
